title: A Skipped Test Is a Withdrawal: Make Agent Patches Deposit a Property Before You Freeze a Flake
author: Finley Zhou
summary: The cheapest way to make an agent patch go green is to skip a test. Most gates allow that skip with no compensating deposit, and then let the skip follow the patch into the next patch in the merge queue. Two weeks later nobody can tell whether the suite shrank because the code got safer or because eleven freezes quietly accumulated. This post proposes a freeze ledger with four blocking rules: a bounded expiry window, a named owner, a compensating property that must actually run against the patch, and a hard ban on inheriting skips across patch boundaries. All four are enforced by a script short enough to read in one pass. The artifact is a policy file plus roughly sixty lines of Python, not a testing framework. 1. The two ways a freeze lies A freeze is a claim that the skipped test was not carrying unique coverage. That claim fails silently in two specific ways. Inheritance. In a merge queue, patch B's gate reuses the artifact from patch A's run. A's skip set rides along, so B is validated against a suite that neither B's author nor B's reviewer chose. The green badge is real; the denominator behind it is not. Withdrawal without deposit. A skipped test stops paying rent. If nothing else asserts its invariant, the patch covers strictly less than the previous commit while reporting the same status. Nothing in a standard CI log distinguishes this from a clean run. Neither failure is loud. Both are visible in one artifact you are probably not writing: the exact set of tests the gate skipped, tied to the commit that skipped them. 2. Step 1: make the freeze a reviewed record, not an inline decorator An inline @pytest.mark.skip lives in the test file, far from the diff a reviewer is reading. Move the decision into one file that changes as its own diff. { "schema" : 1 , "max_window_days" : 14 , "freezes" : [ { "test_id" : "tests/test_billing.py::test_proration_rounding" , "reason" : "order-dependent failure in full suite; passes in isolation" , "owner" : "finley" , "opened" : "2026-10-12" , "expires" : "2026-10-26" , "invariant" : "proration amount never decreases when the period lengthens" , "compensating_property" : "tests/props/test_proration_props.py::test_monotonic_in_period" , "reused_property" : false } ] } Six of those fields are boring on purpose. The two that matter are invariant , written in words, and compensating_property , which must be a real node id. An agent patch that wants to skip a test now shows up in review as a ledger diff plus a property file. That is a reviewable claim; a decorator buried in line 214 is not. The 14-day window is a policy choice, not a discovered constant. Pick a number your team can staff, then let expiry force re-attestation. 3. Step 2: validate shape, owner, and window The first gate is pure bookkeeping. It rejects freezes that cannot be reviewed because nobody owns them, or that have already outlived their window. # audit_freezes.py (reference implementation, not benchmarked) import datetime , json , pathlib , sys FIELDS = ( ' test_id ' , ' reason ' , ' owner ' , ' opened ' , ' expires ' , ' invariant ' , ' compensating_property ' ) def load ( path ): return json . loads ( pathlib . Path ( path ). read_text ())[ ' freezes ' ] def shape_problems ( entry , today , max_window ): problems = [ f ' missing { f } ' for f in FIELDS if not entry . get ( f )] opened = datetime . date . fromisoformat ( entry [ ' opened ' ]) expires = datetime . date . fromisoformat ( entry [ ' expires ' ]) if expires < today : problems . append ( ' expired ' ) if ( expires - opened ). days > max_window : problems . append ( f ' window { ( expires - opened ). days } d exceeds { max_window } d ' ) return problems Run it with an injected date so the check is deterministic in CI: python audit_freezes.py --ledger gate/freeze_ledger.json --today 2026-10-18 An expired freeze should fail the build, not emit a warning. A warning on a skipped test is the same as no gate at all, because the merge button stays green. 4. Step 3: require a deposit that actually runs Here is where most freeze policies stop being useful. A compensating_property string proves nothing unless the property ran in this patch's gate and consumed more than one input. Two automated checks handle that. First, the property must be collected and it must appear in the patch diff: import subprocess , sys def collected_ids ( root = ' . ' ): out = subprocess . run ( [ sys . executable , ' -m ' , ' pytest ' , ' --collect-only ' , ' -q ' , ' --no-header ' ], capture_output = True , text = True , cwd = root , ) return { ln . strip () for ln in out . stdout . splitlines () if ' :: ' in ln } def changed_files ( base = ' origin/main ' ): out = subprocess . run ( [ ' git ' , ' diff ' , ' --name-only ' , f ' { base } ...HEAD ' ], capture_output = True , text = True , check = True , ) return { ln . strip () for ln in out . stdout . splitlines () if ln . strip ()} def deposit_problems ( entry , ids , changed ): pid = entry [ ' compensating_property ' ] problems = [] if pid not in ids : problems . append ( f ' property not collected: { pid } ' ) prop_file = pid . split ( ' :: ' )[ 0 ] if prop_file not in changed and not entry . get ( ' reused_property ' ): problems . append ( ' deposit does not appear in the patch diff ' ) return problems Second, the property must exercise a non-degenerate input space. Count distinct inputs per session and fail below a threshold you pick explicitly: # tests/props/conftest.py import json , pathlib _seen = set () def record ( value ): _seen . add ( repr ( value )) def pytest_sessionfinish ( session , exitstatus ): out = pathlib . Path ( ' gate/prop_samples.json ' ) out . parent . mkdir ( exist_ok = True ) out . write_text ( json . dumps ({ ' distinct ' : len ( _seen )})) python audit_freezes.py --check-deposits \ --ledger gate/freeze_ledger.json \ --samples gate/prop_samples.json \ --min-distinct 8 A property that ran once, on one hardcoded tuple, is a renamed example test. Set --min-distinct low, but set it. 5. Step 4: refuse inherited skips in the merge queue Each gate run writes the skips it actually applied. The queue script then compares parent and child sets and refuses anything the child did not re-derive from the ledger at its own commit. import json , pathlib , sys def freeze_ids ( ledger_path ): return { e [ ' test_id ' ] for e in json . loads ( pathlib . Path ( ledger_path ). read_text ())[ ' freezes ' ]} def refuse_inherited ( parent_skips , child_derived , allow = ()): inherited = set ( parent_skips ) - set ( child_derived ) - set ( allow ) if inherited : sys . exit ( f ' child gate skipped without re-attestation: { sorted ( inherited ) } ' ) The allow set exists for the one legitimate case: a freeze pinned to a release branch with a named approver. Everything else must be re-derived, which costs one pytest --collect-only per queued patch. The ledger is applied by one hook, and the hook records what it did: # conftest.py def pytest_collection_modifyitems ( config , items ): if not config . getoption ( ' --apply-freezes ' ): return frozen = freeze_ids ( ' gate/freeze_ledger.json ' ) applied = [] for item in items : if item . nodeid in frozen : item . add_marker ( pytest . mark . skip ( reason = ' frozen: see gate/freeze_ledger.json ' )) applied . append ( item . nodeid ) pathlib . Path ( ' gate/skipped.json ' ). write_text ( json . dumps ( sorted ( applied ))) 6. Decision table Situation Freeze allowed Required deposit Fails only under parallel execution, passes serially Yes, 14 days Property asserting the invariant plus an isolation test Slow integration test on shared staging No Move it to a nightly lane instead Assertion on log message text Yes, 7 days Structured event assertion replacing the string match Fails only on one CI OS Yes, 14 days, owner is the OS lane maintainer Property run on that OS lane The property itself is flaky No Fix the generator; you cannot deposit a flake Suspicion of a real race No Freezing hides a bug you already found 7. Where the agent, and the hosted run, fit The drafting step is where a model helps. Give it the invariant text and the frozen test, and ask for three candidate properties plus the one input class it would not generate. It will produce plausible candidates; it will not tell you which are weak, so the distinct-input counter and the diff check stay yours. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. The operator reports that MonkeyCode offers free model access and a free server option. In this workflow the model side is the candidate-property drafter, and the server side is where you would run the repeated property checks so the gate does not depend on one laptop. Measure the actual limits yourself before making either a dependency; nothing here assumes a quota, hardware spec, or duration, and I have not benchmarked them. 8. Limitations and who should not adopt this The ledger needs a merge queue or at least a shared branch to be meaningful. A solo repo with direct pushes gets the bookkeeping cost without the inheritance check. prop_samples.json counts distinct repr values. That catches the single-input property, not a weak generator that produces near-duplicates. The property-file-in-diff rule assumes one property per invariant. Splitting an invariant across two files needs a manual note in the ledger. If your flakiness comes from shared staging infrastructure, freezing just relocates the flake. Fix the lane or move the test to a nightly run. Teams that cannot staff a two-week expiry review should delete the flaky test outright and write the property. A freeze nobody revisits is worse than a deletion, because deletion is honest. 9. What to measure after a week Three numbers, all cheap: how many existing freezes fail the deposit check, the median age of open freezes, and how many inherited skips the queue script refused. I am not going to invent those numbers for you — they depend entirely on how much debt your suite is already carrying. Start with one repository and one rule: no freeze without a property that ran. Everything else in this post is enforcement around that sentence.

title: 48-Hour Field Notes: My Race Condition Vanished on a Free Server — It Was Just Slower
author: Taylor Wang
summary: The green run that almost fooled me On Wednesday I moved a flaky test off my laptop and onto a remote box, and it passed 200 times in a row. For about an hour I believed I had accidentally fixed something, which is a dangerous thing to believe at 2 a.m. The test was a concurrent append to a small ledger file, and on my laptop it failed roughly one run in fifteen. So what did the move actually change — the code, the data, or just the shape of the machine underneath it? Nothing in the code changed. That is the whole point of this post: the failure rate of a timing-sensitive bug is a property of the environment , not of your test name. If you only ever run the repro on one machine, you are measuring that machine's scheduler, not your program's correctness. What I actually did in the first twelve hours I stopped trying to "reproduce the bug faster" and started trying to reproduce the sensitivity instead. Three things happened, in this order: I wrote down the exact conditions of the original failure (laptop, on battery, browser open, test file unmodified for six days). I ran the same test 200 times on the remote box and got zero failures, which I initially misread as "not reproducible." I built a sweep that runs the test under deliberately worse scheduling conditions, because the remote box was simply too forgiving. That third step is the one I would repeat. The rest was mostly me arguing with my own assumptions. The artifact: a scheduler-sensitivity sweep Here is the harness, stripped down. It does not try to find the bug; it tries to find the profile under which the bug is willing to appear. #!/usr/bin/env bash # sweep.sh — run one test under several scheduling profiles set -u RUNS = " ${ RUNS :- 200 } " TEST_CMD = " ${ TEST_CMD :- python -m pytest tests/test_ledger.py ::test_concurrent_append -q } " run_profile () { local name = " $1 " ; shift local fails = 0 for _ in $( seq 1 " $RUNS " ) ; do if ! " $@ " > /dev/null 2>&1 ; then fails = $(( fails + 1 )) ; fi done printf '%-14s %s/%s failed\n' " $name " " $fails " " $RUNS " } run_profile "default" bash -c " $TEST_CMD " run_profile "one-core" taskset -c 0 bash -c " $TEST_CMD " run_profile "tight-gil" env PY_SWITCH_INTERVAL = 0.000001 bash -c " $TEST_CMD " run_profile "cpu-starved" cpulimit -l 15 -- bash -c " $TEST_CMD " The tight-gil profile needs one line of glue in conftest.py , because there is no environment variable for sys.setswitchinterval out of the box: # conftest.py import os import sys if ( raw : = os . getenv ( " PY_SWITCH_INTERVAL " )): sys . setswitchinterval ( float ( raw )) Then, before trusting any of it, I check that the profile actually took effect on this machine. A profile that silently does nothing is worse than no profile at all. # probe.py — is this box coarse or fine grained right now? import statistics import sys import threading import time def median_gap_ms ( n : int = 2000 ) -> float : hits : list [ int ] = [] def worker () -> None : for _ in range ( n ): hits . append ( time . perf_counter_ns ()) t = threading . Thread ( target = worker ) t . start () worker () t . join () gaps = [ b - a for a , b in zip ( hits , hits [ 1 :])] return statistics . median ( gaps ) / 1e6 print ( f " switchinterval= { sys . getswitchinterval () * 1e3 : . 3 f } ms " f " median_gap= { median_gap_ms () : . 3 f } ms " ) My result table looks like this shape, and yours will have different numbers in it: profile failures ----------------------- default <n1>/200 one-core <n2>/200 tight-gil <n3>/200 cpu-starved <n4>/200 The shape is the finding, not the digits. If default is clean and one constrained profile is not, your bug is scheduling-sensitive and your fast machine has been lying to you by omission. Where free model access and a free server actually helped The remote box here was MonkeyCode's free server option, and the model I used for a second opinion was their free model access; both are operator-supplied availability claims, and I am describing my own use rather than a spec. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Two uses were genuinely useful, and a third was a trap: Useful: drafting additional budget profiles for the sweep, which I then reviewed line by line before running anything. Useful: running the 800-run sweep off my laptop, so a sleeping lid or a browser tab could not contaminate the timing I was trying to measure. A trap: asking a model to "fix" the race directly. It produced a plausible lock that serialized the whole ledger and made the test pass by deleting the concurrency it was supposed to verify. That last point matters more than the first two. Free access to a model is cheap; free access to a critic that does not get to commit is the actual workflow. What broke, and what I would not repeat Wall-clock timestamps in the test assertions. They passed on the slow box and failed on the fast one, for reasons unrelated to the bug. Treating a clean 200-run sweep as proof. Zero failures under one profile is one data point about one scheduler. Running the sweep in CI first. CI is shared and noisy, so I could not tell whether a failure came from the bug or a neighbor. I also had to stop myself from quoting the sweep's timings as performance data. The free server may be shared, so latency numbers from it describe contention on that host and nothing about your code — a lesson I apparently need to relearn periodically. A short decision table Question you are asking Laptop Free remote box Constrained local profile Does it fail at all? Yes, sometimes Sometimes not Best chance Is it scheduling-sensitive? Hard to say No Yes How fast is my code? Noisy No — shared host No Can I run 800 iterations cheaply? Battery dies Usually fine Fine Who should not do this Do not use this sweep if your defect is deterministic, because you will burn a day measuring a scheduler that was never involved. Do not use it if you need real throughput numbers, since a shared free host cannot give them to you. And do not run it against anything holding production credentials, because a remote box you did not provision is the wrong place for secrets. What I would repeat on Monday Build the sensitivity sweep before the fix, run it somewhere your laptop cannot interfere, and keep the model in the reviewer's chair instead of the committer's chair. If a green run on a new machine ever reassures you, ask the obvious question first: did the bug go away, or did the timing? If you run the sweep yourself, I would like to know which profile finally reproduced your bug — that is the setting I want to steal.

title: Five Myths About Retrying an LLM Call, and the Fault-Injection Drill That Tests Them
author: Jordan Huang
summary: Your retry loop is maybe eight lines. Why does it double your bill and duplicate side effects? I keep seeing the same pattern in reviews. The retry logic looks correct, and everyone stops reading there. That is the problem. Retries are where cost, correctness, and latency quietly disagree. Below are five claims I hear often, the evidence that breaks them, and a small drill you can run in an afternoon. Label: the code here is a template, not a benchmark. I have not run it against your stack. Run the drill yourself and trust your own numbers, not mine. Myth 1: "A retry is basically free" A retry is not a repeat. It is a second request with the same input. You pay to send the prompt again, on every attempt. Long system prompts make this expensive fast. Corrected model: retry cost scales with input_tokens × attempts × concurrent_callers . Measure attempts, not errors. Ask yourself: does your dashboard count attempts, or only final outcomes? Most count outcomes. Myth 2: "HTTP 200 means the model finished" A 200 means the transport succeeded. It says nothing about the answer. Truncated completions, empty content, and stream cuts all arrive as 200. Your retry loop never fires. Corrected model: treat finish_reason , content length, and schema validity as part of the success check. A response is not a result. How many of your retries are actually triggered by business-level incompleteness? Usually zero. Myth 3: "Exponential backoff with jitter is enough" Backoff controls timing. It does not control volume. If every caller retries four times, a partial outage becomes a full one. Jitter spreads the pain, not the load. Corrected model: add a retry budget per request and per minute. Cap total attempts across the fleet. Rules that survive contact with production: Retry 429 and 5xx only. Never retry 400 or 401 . Honor Retry-After when present. It beats your formula. Stop after a fixed attempt count. Then fail over or fail closed. Emit one metric per attempt, tagged by error class. Myth 4: "Retrying is idempotent because the call is stateless" The model call is stateless. Your handler is not. If the tool call wrote a ticket, charged a card, or sent mail, a retry repeats the side effect. Corrected model: retries are only safe behind an idempotency key or a commit barrier. The barrier is a local check: did the side effect already happen? Rhetorical but useful: what would your retry loop do to a payment webhook twice in a row? Myth 5: "You can resume a stream where it stopped" You cannot resume mid-token. The connection is gone, and so is the partial state. What you can do is checkpoint at message boundaries. Re-request with the completed prefix as context. Corrected model: streams are not resumable transports. They are progress signals. Persist what you received, then decide. The drill: inject faults, count attempts This is the part that changes minds. Ten minutes of setup, one table of evidence. The stub server uses only the standard library. No dependencies, no keys. # stub_server.py - deterministic fault injection, Python 3.9+ import json , threading from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler , ThreadingHTTPServer FAULTS = [ " ok " , " truncate " , " 500 " , " 429 " , " slow " ] state = { " n " : 0 } lock = threading . Lock () class H ( BaseHTTPRequestHandler ): def do_POST ( self ): self . rfile . read ( int ( self . headers . get ( " Content-Length " , 0 ))) with lock : fault = FAULTS [ state [ " n " ] % len ( FAULTS )] state [ " n " ] += 1 if fault == " 500 " : self . send_response ( 500 ); self . end_headers () self . wfile . write ( b ' { " error " : " boom " } ' ); return if fault == " 429 " : self . send_response ( 429 ) self . send_header ( " Retry-After " , " 1 " ); self . end_headers (); return body = { " choices " : [{ " message " : { " role " : " assistant " , " content " : " ok " }, " finish_reason " : " length " if fault == " truncate " else " stop " , }]} raw = json . dumps ( body ). encode () self . send_response ( 200 ) self . send_header ( " Content-Type " , " application/json " ) self . send_header ( " Content-Length " , str ( len ( raw ))) self . end_headers () self . wfile . write ( raw ) def log_message ( self , * args ): pass if __name__ == " __main__ " : ThreadingHTTPServer (( " 127.0.0.1 " , 8787 ), H ). serve_forever () Now the client. It records every attempt in a ledger. # drill.py - counts attempts and re-sent input per call import json , random , time , urllib . error , urllib . request URL = " http://127.0.0.1:8787/v1/chat " PROMPT = " summarise this ticket in one line " # swap for a real payload def classify ( code , body ): if code == 429 : return " throttle " if code >= 500 or code == 0 : return " transient " if code == 200 and body [ " choices " ][ 0 ][ " finish_reason " ] == " length " : return " truncated " return " ok " def call_once (): req = urllib . request . Request ( URL , data = json . dumps ({ " prompt " : PROMPT }). encode (), headers = { " Content-Type " : " application/json " }, ) try : with urllib . request . urlopen ( req , timeout = 5 ) as r : return r . status , json . loads ( r . read ()) except urllib . error . HTTPError as e : return e . code , {} except Exception : return 0 , {} def drill ( cases = 10 , budget = 4 ): ledger = [] for _ in range ( cases ): input_tokens = len ( PROMPT . split ()) # crude proxy, use real usage for attempt in range ( 1 , budget + 1 ): code , body = call_once () cls = classify ( code , body ) ledger . append ({ " attempt " : attempt , " code " : code , " class " : cls , " input_resent " : input_tokens }) if cls in ( " ok " , " truncated " ): break delay = min ( 2 ** attempt * 0.1 , 1.0 ) time . sleep ( delay * random . uniform ( 0.5 , 1.5 )) return ledger if __name__ == " __main__ " : rows = drill () print ( json . dumps ( rows , indent = 2 )) print ( " attempts: " , len ( rows )) print ( " input tokens re-sent: " , sum ( r [ " input_resent " ] for r in rows )) Run it: python stub_server.py & python drill.py | tail -n 2 Then read the ledger. Do you see attempts your old loop would have skipped? Do you see truncated responses marked as success? The decision table I actually use Signal Retry? Action 429 with Retry-After Once Sleep the header value, then one attempt 5xx Yes, budgeted Backoff with jitter, cap at 3 Timeout, no response Yes, budgeted Same route first, then failover 400 / 401 Never Fix the request or the credential finish_reason = length No Raise the limit or chunk the input Empty content Once Retry, then fail closed Where MonkeyCode fits in this drill A fault drill needs two things: a stub server and a second route to fail over to. MonkeyCode's free model access gives me that second route without a card. The operator-supplied free server option can host the stub, so the drill does not touch production networking. I would not run the whole harness blindly there. Check the current quotas and limits yourself first. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Use it as the failover target you test against, not as the reason the drill exists. The drill works with any second endpoint. Limitations, and who should skip this The stub returns fixed shapes. It tests your control flow, not model quality. Token counts in the script are a proxy. Swap in real usage numbers. Retry budgets need tuning per route. One global number hides the problem. Skip this if you have a single caller and no side effects. You have bigger wins elsewhere. Skip it too if your platform already enforces retry budgets and idempotency keys. Audit those settings instead. What changes after the drill You stop treating retries as error handling. You start treating them as load, cost, and duplicate-work decisions. That reframing is the whole payoff. The eight-line loop stays short, but now it has a reason for every line. What would your ledger show tomorrow?

title: Bulk Google + Amazon keyword search volume for about $3 per 1,000 keywords (API, n8n, Claude)
author: Pravinraj Vincent
summary: If you've ever pasted 300 keywords into an SEO suite and hit a daily cap, or you just want search volume inside a script or an AI agent without paying for a seat, this is the setup I use: one API call in, one row per keyword out. What you get per keyword Google monthly search volume, with up to 4 years of monthly history CPC, competition, keyword difficulty and search intent Month-over-month, quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year trend Amazon monthly search volume (a modeled estimate, because Amazon doesn't publish volumes) An optional USPTO trademark-risk flag, useful if you sell on Etsy, Merch by Amazon or KDP The data comes from DataForSEO. Google figures come from its Google Ads-based keyword database (refreshed about monthly), so no Google Ads account is needed. A real run: 12 keywords, United States I mixed SEO-tool keywords with product keywords to show the range: Keyword Google / month Amazon / month CPC KD YoY Trademark flag google keyword planner 49,500 5,759 $18.10 47 -18% high ("google") keyword research tool 4,400 299 $15.75 81 -81% none etsy seo 2,900 224 $7.69 22 -47% high ("etsy") long tail keywords 1,000 149 $46.37 61 -70% none keyword search volume 880 74 $12.61 79 -55% none amazon keyword tool 260 74 $12.83 17 -77% none coloring book for adults 60,500 1,907 $0.61 1 -18% none teacher gift 18,100 1,645 $0.88 0 0% none pickleball paddle 301,000 11,594 $1.50 25 -45% medium Three things stood out: Generic "keyword tool" searches are falling fast. "keyword research tool" is down 81% year over year and "free keyword tool" is down 80%. My guess is that people now ask an AI assistant instead. That's also the best argument for piping keyword data into those assistants (see below). CPC and difficulty don't move together. "long tail keywords" has a $46 CPC but KD 61. "amazon keyword tool" has a $12.83 CPC at KD 17, a much easier target. The trademark flag isn't noise for sellers. "etsy seo" and "google keyword planner" come back high-risk because of live marks. That's irrelevant for a blog post, but it matters if the phrase goes on a T-shirt. "pickleball paddle" is medium because live marks contain "pickleball". That doesn't mean you can't use it. It means you should check the record before printing it. Option 1: Python from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( " <YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN> " ) run = client . actor ( " vncntlabs/keyword-search-volume " ). call ( run_input = { " keywords " : [ " teacher gift " , " coloring book for adults " , " pickleball paddle " ], " sources " : [ " google " , " amazon " ], " location " : " United States " , " trademarkCheck " : True , }) for row in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items (): print ( row [ " keyword " ], row [ " googleSearchVolume " ], row [ " amazonSearchVolume " ], row [ " cpcUsd " ]) Option 2: plain HTTP (n8n, Make, Zapier, curl) curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/vncntlabs~keyword-search-volume/run-sync-get-dataset-items" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $APIFY_TOKEN " -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"keywords":["teacher gift","pickleball paddle"],"sources":["google"],"location":"United States"}' In n8n, that's one HTTP Request node, or the Apify node with "Run actor and get dataset". Option 3: from Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor (MCP) Apify runs a hosted MCP server. Add it to your client: { "mcpServers" : { "apify" : { "url" : "https://mcp.apify.com" } } } Then ask something like "Get US Google and Amazon search volume for these 40 keywords and sort by volume per KD point." The assistant finds the Actor, runs it, and reads the dataset. You pay only for the rows returned. What it costs Event Price Keyword with Google volume $0.003 Keyword with Amazon volume $0.004 Batch fee (per up to 700 Google / 1,000 Amazon keywords that returned data) $0.05 Trademark check $0.001 So 1,000 Google-only keywords cost $3.10 , and keywords with no data aren't charged. The 12-keyword run above with Google, Amazon and trademark checks came to about $0.20 at list price. You can set a maximum charge per run, and the Actor stops before exceeding it. A new Apify account's free monthly credit covers a few hundred keywords. To be fair to the competition: if you only need Google numbers for very large lists, some Store Actors charge less per row (I keep a dated comparison on our site). Where this one is different is Amazon volume and the trademark flag in the same row. Caveats Volumes are rounded monthly averages, so use them to compare keywords, not as exact traffic. Amazon volume is modeled, so treat it as relative. Trademark flags are automated screening against live U.S. federal marks only. They're not legal advice, and no flag doesn't mean safe. title: Migrating books between providers: tying opening balances to bank statements, with uncleared items
author: Damin Mutti
summary: When books move between providers, the new ledger opens with the old provider's last balance sheet. Each bank and card balance on it must equal the bank's printed statement for that day, plus or minus uncleared items such as an uncashed check. The rule is difference = 0 . An unexplained gap means the old books need another look first. That is a data validation problem with a very clear rule, so it is worth writing as code. I work on ZeraBooks, where we set opening balances this way for businesses moving from Bench and elsewhere. All figures below are fictional. What data do you need for an opening balance tie-out? Two sources per account: the closing balance sheet from the old provider, and the printed statement balance from the bank, both on the cutover date. from dataclasses import dataclass , field from decimal import Decimal as D @dataclass class OpeningAccount : name : str books : D # old provider's balance sheet at cutover statement : D # bank's printed balance on the same date uncleared : list [ tuple [ str , D ]] = field ( default_factory = list ) # each item: (description, signed amount as it affects the bank) Use Decimal , not floats. A one-cent mismatch from binary rounding looks exactly like a real one-cent error, and you will lose an afternoon to it. What is the rule for tying opening balances to a statement? For a bank account, the statement balance plus the uncleared items must equal the books balance. A check written on December 29 reduces the books immediately but has not reached the bank, so it appears as a negative uncleared item. def tie_out ( a : OpeningAccount ) -> D : explained = a . statement + sum (( amt for _ , amt in a . uncleared ), D ( " 0 " )) return a . books - explained # must be zero How does a clean cutover look in code? accounts = [ OpeningAccount ( " Business checking " , D ( " 18420.55 " ), D ( " 18970.55 " ), [( " Check #1043, written Dec 29 " , D ( " -550.00 " ))]), OpeningAccount ( " Savings " , D ( " 25000.00 " ), D ( " 25000.00 " )), OpeningAccount ( " Business credit card " , D ( " -2316.40 " ), D ( " -2316.40 " )), OpeningAccount ( " Equipment loan " , D ( " -14800.00 " ), D ( " -14800.00 " )), ] for a in accounts : gap = tie_out ( a ) print ( f " { a . name : 24 } { ' OK ' if gap == 0 else f ' UNEXPLAINED { gap } ' } " ) All four print OK : Account Books, Dec 31 Statement, Dec 31 Uncleared Gap Business checking 18,420.55 18,970.55 -550.00 (check #1043) 0.00 Savings 25,000.00 25,000.00 0.00 Business credit card -2,316.40 -2,316.40 0.00 Equipment loan -14,800.00 -14,800.00 0.00 Checking is $550.00 higher at the bank, and the uncleared check explains all of it. The opening balance stays at the books figure, $18,420.55, and the check is carried forward as an outstanding item so the first month's reconciliation picks it up when it clears. The same rule in the ZeraBooks opening books screen: one uncleared check explains the whole gap, so the account shows Agrees. What does an unexplained gap look like? Change one input. Suppose the card statement shows -2516.40 and nobody can point to a pending charge. Business credit card UNEXPLAINED 200.00 Now stop. Don't plug the $200.00 to an equity account and carry on. The difference was created in some month the old provider closed, and the cheapest time to find it is now, before twelve new months are layered on top. Walk back month by month, comparing the ledger balance with each statement's printed close, until you find the first month the gap appears. Which checks do people skip? Same date on both sides. A balance sheet dated December 31 compared with a statement that closes on December 27 will never tie, and the "difference" is four days of activity. Match statement periods to the cutover date, or use the bank's daily balance for that date. Sign conventions. Liabilities come out of most balance sheet exports as positive numbers and out of most statements as negative ones, or the reverse. Normalise once at load time, not inside the comparison. def normalise ( amount : D , is_liability : bool , export_positive : bool ) -> D : return - amount if ( is_liability and export_positive ) else amount What happens after the tie-out? Only once every account returns zero do the opening balances go into the new ledger. From there, each month is proven the same way: statement opening plus lines equals statement closing, opening equals last month's closing, and the ledger equals the printed close. The full move off Bench, including what to download before you leave and which months are worth re-checking, is on the ZeraBooks page about moving your books off Bench . Key takeaways Opening balances come from the old provider's last closed balance sheet , dated the same day as the statements you compare. The rule per account: books minus (statement plus uncleared items) must equal 0.00 . Use Decimal and normalise signs once, at load time. An unexplained gap gets traced back to the month it first appears. Never plug it to equity. FAQ Should the opening balance be the books figure or the bank figure? The books figure. In the example, checking opens at $18,420.55, and the $550.00 check is carried as an outstanding item until it clears. What if the old provider's balance sheet and the statement have different dates? They will never tie. Use statements that close on the cutover date, or the bank's daily balance for that day. Does this need a bank feed? No. Everything here runs from the printed statement balances in the PDFs. ZeraBooks has no bank feed either; it works from uploaded statements. Disclosure: I'm on the ZeraBooks team. Our done-for-you bookkeeping services run this tie-out for new clients from their uploaded statements, from $150 a month in U.S. dollars, priced after a free call.

title: Is my Supabase database public? A 5-minute check with the anon key
author: FixLoop
summary: If you shipped a Lovable (or any Supabase) app, your anon key is in the browser. That's fine, it's supposed to be. The real question is different: can a stranger read your tables with that key and no login? If Row Level Security is off on a table that still has grants to anon , the answer is yes. Here's a 5-minute check you can run on your own project. Why the anon key isn't the leak The anon key is a public JWT. Postgres then decides what it can do in two layers: Grants decide whether anon can SELECT / INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE the table at all. RLS decides which rows survive that grant. RLS off means the second layer never runs. If anon also has a grant (the old default on public tables), every row is reachable from the REST endpoint. A policy of using (true) is the same hole with RLS "on": the dashboard badge looks fine, the table is still public. The check Open your live app in a private window, DevTools → Network, filter rest/v1 . Grab the project host ( abcdefghij.supabase.co ), a table name from the path, and the apikey header from a signed-out request. Never use the service_role key for this (or anywhere in the client). curl "https://YOUR_PROJECT.supabase.co/rest/v1/YOUR_TABLE?select=*&limit=5" \ -H "apikey: YOUR_ANON_KEY" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_ANON_KEY" No cookies, no session. If this returns user data, anyone can do it too. Reading the result 200 + rows : anon can read the table. RLS is off or a policy allows anonymous SELECT. Fix this first. 200 + [] : there's a SELECT grant but no rows passed RLS (or the table is empty). Retry on a table you know has data. If the signed-in app shows rows and anon still gets [] , you're probably fine. 401 : bad or truncated key. This does not mean the table is private. 403 / 42501 : anon has no grant, so the request never reaches RLS. After Oct 30, 2026 this shows up a lot on new tables ( why ). 404 / PGRST205 : wrong table name. Use the one from the network tab. The safe fix Turn RLS on and scope policies to auth.uid() . Don't "fix" an open table by granting more. alter table public . your_table enable row level security ; create policy "select own rows" on public . your_table for select to authenticated using ( auth . uid () = user_id ); create policy "insert own rows" on public . your_table for insert to authenticated with check ( auth . uid () = user_id ); grant select , insert , update , delete on table public . your_table to authenticated ; Don't do any of these: GRANT ALL ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO anon; any grant to anon while RLS is off using (true) on a table with private rows the service_role key in frontend env In Lovable, put the same rules in your project instructions so the next migration doesn't recreate the hole. Full guide The longer version with the browser-console variant, a checklist, and an FAQ (should I rotate the anon key? Lovable says RLS is on, can it still be public?) is here: https://fixloop.dev/guides/is-my-supabase-database-public I run FixLoop . There's a free scan for leaked keys and missing headers, and we fix broken Lovable/Supabase apps for a fixed price. No fix, no pay.

title: How to Choose a Pediatrician Your Child Can Rely on Through Every Stage of Childhood
author: marilious mari
summary: Choosing a pediatrician involves more than finding a nearby medical office. Parents need a healthcare professional who understands their child’s developmental needs, communicates clearly, and helps them make informed decisions about everything from routine checkups to unexpected illnesses. The right relationship can make healthcare less stressful and give families a dependable source of guidance as their children grow. For families in Utah Valley, comparing pediatric practices carefully can help ensure that a child receives consistent, age-appropriate care. Understanding what to look for before scheduling the first appointment makes it easier to find a provider who fits both the child’s needs and the family’s daily routine. Look Beyond Location When Comparing Pediatric Practices Convenience matters, especially when a child has a fever or needs a same-day appointment. However, distance should not be the only factor when choosing a pediatrician. Parents should also consider the practice’s medical services, appointment availability, communication methods, and approach to preventive care. Start by checking whether the office provides routine wellness visits, immunizations, developmental screenings, and treatment for common childhood illnesses. Families with infants may need frequent weight checks and feeding guidance, while parents of school-aged children may prioritize sports physicals, behavioral concerns, or help managing recurring conditions. It is also worth asking how the practice handles urgent concerns outside regular office hours. Some offices offer nurse advice lines or after-hours guidance, while others direct families to urgent care facilities. Knowing these arrangements in advance can prevent confusion when a child becomes sick unexpectedly. Parents should also consider practical details such as parking, office hours, insurance acceptance, and the availability of online appointment scheduling. A practice that fits a family's routine is often easier to maintain over the long term. Understand the Importance of Preventive Care Children change quickly, and their healthcare needs evolve with each stage of development. Regular well-child visits help pediatricians monitor growth, review developmental milestones, discuss nutrition, and identify concerns that may benefit from early attention. For infants, appointments often focus on feeding, sleep, weight gain, and early development. During the preschool years, parents may have questions about speech, behavior, social skills, and readiness for school. Older children may need guidance on physical activity, emotional well-being, puberty, and healthy habits. Preventive visits also give parents an opportunity to discuss concerns that may not seem urgent but still deserve attention. Keeping an updated record of immunizations, previous illnesses, medications, and developmental observations can make these conversations more productive. When evaluating a practice, ask whether the provider encourages questions and explains recommendations in understandable language. A good pediatric appointment should leave parents with a clearer understanding of their child's health and any recommended next steps. Find a Provider Who Understands Your Child's Individual Needs Every child has a different temperament, medical history, and developmental pattern. Some children feel comfortable around healthcare professionals, while others become anxious during examinations. A pediatrician who communicates patiently and adapts the appointment to the child's needs can help make visits more manageable. Parents looking for a family pediatrician in Utah Valley should consider whether the practice can support their child's needs from infancy through adolescence. Pediatric Care+ serves families in the Utah County area, including Provo and Orem, and provides services such as wellness visits, immunizations, developmental assessments, and treatment for childhood illnesses. Beyond the range of services, consider how the provider approaches communication. Does the doctor listen carefully before making recommendations? Are treatment options explained clearly? Can parents raise concerns about behavior, learning difficulties, sleep, or nutrition without feeling rushed? These questions are particularly important when a child has an ongoing health condition that requires regular monitoring. Consistent communication can help families understand treatment plans, recognize changes in symptoms, and coordinate specialist care when necessary. It is also helpful to ask whether children can continue seeing a familiar provider as they grow. While scheduling needs and provider availability may vary, continuity can help build trust and give clinicians a better understanding of a child's medical history. Prepare for the First Appointment A little preparation can make a child's first visit more efficient and less stressful. Before the appointment, gather relevant medical records, immunization history, medication details, and information about previous diagnoses or allergies. Parents can also write down questions in advance. This is especially useful when several concerns need attention during one visit. Consider asking about: Which preventive appointments and immunizations are recommended for your child's age. How to schedule appointments for sudden illnesses. What options are available for after-hours medical guidance. How referrals, prescription renewals, and follow-up visits are handled. Which insurance plans the practice accepts and what costs may apply. For younger children, bringing a familiar toy, comfort item, or snack when appropriate may help reduce anxiety. Teenagers may appreciate having time to discuss certain health concerns privately with their clinician, depending on their age, the situation, and applicable confidentiality rules. Before leaving, make sure you understand any recommended tests, treatments, or follow-up appointments. If instructions are unclear, ask the healthcare team to explain them again. Make a Long-Term Choice, Not Just a Convenient One Choosing a pediatrician is an ongoing decision rather than a one-time appointment. As children develop, families may need different services, additional guidance, or referrals to specialists. A practice that communicates well and provides appropriate preventive and sick care can make these transitions easier. Parents should balance accessibility, medical expertise, communication style, insurance coverage, and the ability to address their child's changing needs. Reading practice information and asking specific questions before enrolling can reveal whether a provider is a practical fit. Ultimately, the best choice is a healthcare professional who takes concerns seriously, explains recommendations clearly, and helps parents participate confidently in their child's care. Establishing that relationship early can support healthier routines and make navigating childhood health concerns more manageable for the entire family.
