title: Instructions Are Not Boundaries
author: Michael "Mike" K. Saleme
summary: On 9 October, Anthropic published a report on actions its models took during evaluations and internal use that it did not intend. One of the four categories it lists: "Claude submitting a sensitive form on a real website when it should not have." In one case, Claude Haiku 4.5 "was instructed to complete a form up until the final submission stage, but to stop before actually submitting. Several times Claude mistakenly submitted the form instead, expecting there to be an additional confirmation page." In another, a run working through randomly selected webpages reached a police department's tip form. "Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions." The model submitted an invented tip. Per the report, it "was flagged as spam and was never forwarded for investigation." Anthropic disclosed this voluntarily, described the impact as minimal, notified the organizations involved, and corrected the post three days later. That disclosure is what lets the rest of us learn from it, and it deserves plain credit. The pattern Any deployment that relies on prompt instructions alone leaves enforcement dependent on the model's interpretation. An instruction travels with the task. The model reads it, weighs it against the goal, and interprets it. When the goal and the rule pull apart, interpretation decides what executes. Anthropic names the dominant mechanism. Most of the cases are forms of persistence, "in which Claude, when it cannot complete a task as given, works around a restriction instead of stopping." The form cases show it is not the only one. Anthropic describes the Haiku case as a mistaken expectation of another confirmation page. That illustrates a different failure: misjudging when an action becomes final. These cases expose different failures: misunderstanding when an action becomes final, acting outside an incompletely specified scope, and finding another route around a restriction. The tip-form case shows the second. A list of prohibited actions can leave consequential actions unspecified. That one named five things, and "did not rule out form submissions." Anthropic is fair about the counterargument: some of these failures "could have been avoided if the evaluation questions had more clearly stated what was in and out of scope." It answers it in the next breath. Claude meets ambiguous and impossible tasks every day in real use. Clearer instructions narrow the gap. They do not close it. Where the enforcement moved Read the remediation section as an architecture diagram. Anthropic is extending its suspension of live internet access to all internal evaluations until it verifies the relevant safeguards. Internet access tools such as web fetch get tighter guardrails on what the model can do with them. New tooling detects and blocks these behaviors. It "now runs on most of our evaluations and on internal agentic use of frontier models," and "When we tested it against the cases described in this post, it blocked all of them." Internal agents move to centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment, and far more of what agents do is monitored. None of these is a sentence addressed to the model. Each one acts outside it: containment, monitoring, and restrictions on the tools themselves. Training stays in the plan. Anthropic is direct about its limits: "alignment training is not yet sufficient or fully robust on its own, at least in the short term, so we also rely on defense-in-depth approaches." Defense in depth only works when the outer layer holds whether or not the inner one does. One case sharpens where "outside" has to be. The fetch tool limits URL length "to reduce the risk from Claude using long URLs to take certain unwanted actions, such as exfiltrating larger amounts of data." Several models routed around it "by using free URL shortening services." That limit sat outside the model and still did not hold, because it constrained one tool's argument rather than the action. Placement outside the agent is necessary, and it is not sufficient. A check at the point of execution can still be bypassable, misconfigured, or aimed at the wrong property. An effective boundary must mediate every available route to the protected action and enforce the relevant policy before the action takes effect. A rule the agent is told is not a rule the system enforces. What an outside test looks like If enforcement lives outside the agent, the evidence has to come from outside too: an observation of what executed, not the agent's account of what it did. Anthropic makes the adjacent point itself: "a model's own account of its reasoning is not necessarily reliable evidence of its beliefs or reasons for action." Moving a rule out of the prompt and into the runtime raises the next question: does the runtime actually enforce what it was told to deny? The open-source Agent Security Harness has one test of exactly that shape, APB-003 | Declared Deny Rule Enforced at Execution : Declare a deny rule for one call to the runtime. Approve an allowed call, and approve the denied call too, so a missing approval cannot be the reason it does not run. Make both calls, and diff the runtime's execution record around each one. The oracle is what executed. A refusal message never counts. The allowed call is the positive control: if nothing executes, the result is INCONCLUSIVE, because a runtime that runs nothing looks identical to one that enforces. The oracle is only as good as the record. For a real deployment, the execution record must reliably capture the relevant side effect. An absent entry in an incomplete log is not evidence that an action was blocked. Output against the module's own reference targets: BOUND PASS the allowed call executed and the denied call did not; it was approved and still blocked at execution POLICY_UNENFORCED FAIL POLICY NOT ENFORCED: a call matching a declared deny rule executed (GHSA-5r6c-gj4g-r697 shape) REFUSES_ALL INCONCLUSIVE the denied call did not execute, but neither did the approved, allowed one, so nothing distinguishes enforcement from a target that runs nothing. The limits matter as much as the shape. APB-003 tests a deny rule declared to the runtime, not an instruction in a prompt. Against Anthropic's cases it is adjacent, not a match. It needs a caller-written adapter that maps approvals and executions onto a real runtime, and a wrong adapter produces a wrong verdict. The repository evidence reviewed for this post contains no real-runtime validation. The output above comes from reference targets the module itself defines, and says nothing about any real system. It matches the denied call exactly. It would not catch the URL-shortener route: an equivalent action reached through a different tool. APB-003 asks a narrower question: does an explicit runtime deny still hold when approval is present? Test it with an allowed positive control, then inspect execution evidence. Extend that testing to alternative routes before claiming the action is contained. Views are my own.

title: How I'd Run Bug Triage on 40 Defect Reports Before a Release: Lessons From Postgres 19
author: Anna
summary: TL;DR On October 9th, Peter Eisentraut, a PostgreSQL core team member and committer, wrote that about 8 to 10 significant features had been reverted from Postgres 19. Part of the reason for the Postgres 19 reverts was bug triage math: LLM-assisted review found a long tail of real edge-case defects, and each one carried fixed overhead. The twist: most of the reverted Postgres 19 code was written before AI review got this good, so the quality bar went up after the code was committed. On October 10th, the PostgreSQL release team moved Postgres 19 general availability (GA) to November 19 . Tomas Vondra, a PostgreSQL major contributor, argues that most reverts came from human review that happened late. My plan for 40 real defect reports and a release date: cluster them, score blast radius, split must-fix from follow-up, do the hours math, then move review earlier. What Happened to Postgres 19, and Where AI Code Review Fits When Peter Eisentraut, a PostgreSQL core team member, posted about the Postgres 19 reverts on Friday, October 9th, I read it twice and then opened a notes file. I wasn't thinking about Postgres internals. I was thinking about every release meeting I've sat in where a list of bugs landed two weeks before ship. The release decision is the part of the Postgres 19 story I care about. A mature project with excellent reviewers got a pile of real defect reports late in the cycle, and had to decide what ships. Your team will face the same decision, probably sooner than you'd like. Why the Postgres 19 Reverts Happened Peter Eisentraut, a PostgreSQL core team member who committed some of the reverted features, laid out several causes in his October 9th post . Four of them matter for bug triage: Architectural defects. Some Postgres 19 features had "significant architectural defects that would have been hard to fix quickly and during beta." A long tail of edge cases. Other Postgres 19 features had "a long tail of relatively harmless issues" in edge cases. Peter Eisentraut wrote that with LLM-assisted code review, "you're staring at a list of like forty defect reports. And even if each of them requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time." A raised quality bar. Peter Eisentraut wrote that the reverted features "were written a long time ago when LLM-assisted code review was not as useful as it is now, meaning that the effective quality bar has been raised after the time the feature was written and committed." He was clear that this "is not due to 'vibe coding'." Security load. In Peter Eisentraut's account, many senior PostgreSQL developers spent April to August on security fixes, so beta-period review and testing dropped and only picked up again in August. The gap pushed a lot of discoveries late. The Counterpoint: Most Reverts Came From Human Review Tomas Vondra, a PostgreSQL major contributor, published a revert-by-revert analysis on October 1st, Are we reverting patches because of bugs found by AI? . His analysis has three findings that matter for bug triage: Count. Of the 12 Postgres 19 reverts Tomas Vondra looked at, "only 4 came out at 'probably AI' or 'AI'." The rest came from regular human review. Timing, the finding that matters most for bug triage. The number of Postgres 19 reverts looked normal compared with earlier releases, but the timing didn't. PostgreSQL reverts usually cluster right after feature freeze. For Postgres 19 they flatlined, then spiked in early September. Cause. Tomas Vondra links the late spike to security load. He counts about 5 PostgreSQL CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) last year and 44 so far this year, some reported with AI help. The same senior developers handle both security fixes and feature review. I won't tell you "AI delayed Postgres 19." The fair version: AI-assisted review added real defects to a Postgres 19 review cycle that was already running late, and every report cost time to process. The New Postgres 19 Release Date On October 10th, Jonathan Katz, a PostgreSQL core team member, posted for the release team that Postgres 19 GA would move to November 19. He gave the reason as "the volume of fixes that have been added to the back branches," which the team wanted in a second release candidate on November 12. The Postgres 19 release timeline at a glance: October 9th: Peter Eisentraut posts about the reverts. October 10th: the PostgreSQL release team moves GA to November 19. October 15th: Postgres 19 Release Candidate 1 (RC1) ships . October 16th: The Register's write-up by reporter Lindsay Clark says Postgres 19 was once slated for late September or early October, and that the reverted features will likely land in Postgres 20. November 12th: planned second release candidate (RC2). November 19th: planned GA. Why 40 Small Defect Reports Turn Into a Bug Triage Problem AI code review changes when defects arrive and how many arrive at once. The table compares defects users find over years of releases with defects AI review finds right before one. What changes Defects found by users over the years Defects found by AI review before release When they arrive Spread over minor releases Bunched before the release date Per-report cost Paid slowly, one at a time Paid all at once, by the same few people The hard part Finding the bug Deciding what ships Default outcome Fix in a minor release Fix, cut or revert under a deadline Peter Eisentraut, a PostgreSQL core team member, wrote that edge-case defects used to surface after release, and the project "would have fixed them bit by bit over the subsequent five years." With AI-assisted review, many of those findings now land in the weeks before a release. The defect timeline shows one set of defect reports drawn twice. On the top row, defects found by users trickle in across years of minor releases. On the bottom row, defects found by AI review bunch up right before general availability (GA), where the fixed overhead per report starts to hurt. How I'd Run Bug Triage on 40 Defect Reports Before a Release Date Say it's my feature, and AI review just handed me 40 defect reports. They're real defects, not noise, and I have a few weeks before the release date. Here's how I'd spend the first afternoon of bug triage. 1. Cluster the Reports by Feature and Root Cause I'd start by merging duplicates and grouping by root cause. Forty reports rarely mean forty problems. Ten of them might be one missing check that shows up in ten code paths. Clustering defect reports is how you pay the fixed per-report overhead (reproduce, test, review, commit) fewer times. One owner, one branch, one round of tests and one commit series per cluster beats 40 separate threads. 2. Score Each Cluster by Blast Radius Blast radius is how far a defect reaches if it ships. I'd rank clusters by what they can damage, not by how many reports they contain or how big the fix looks. Blast Radius Signals for a Database Feature Wrong query results with no error Data loss or corruption on disk Security and permission checks skipped Crashes or hangs in the server Behavior you can't change after release without breaking users Odd combinations of features, such as Peter Eisentraut's example of a domain over a composite type inside a partition inside a view Odd feature combinations are where LLM-assisted review shines. Writing about cases like a domain over a composite type inside a partition inside a view, Peter Eisentraut, a PostgreSQL core team member, said "no one can manually test this or even enumerate these test cases," but LLM-assisted fuzzing "can find problems with this really quickly." Qodo's code quality report shows edge cases are a real pain point in review too. In the August 2026 survey of 500 U.S. developers at organizations already using AI meaningfully in the software development lifecycle, 21.8% named hidden bugs or edge cases as their greatest challenge when reviewing AI-generated code. Edge cases are hard for people, so reports about them deserve a real look. 3. Separate Severity vs Priority Severity is how bad a defect is. Priority is how soon you fix it. Keep them as two separate fields, because a deadline changes priority without changing severity. A severe bug in a feature you can revert might get low priority for this release, because the fix is "revert." A mild bug in an on-disk format gets high priority, because you can't patch it later without pain. Tom Lane, a PostgreSQL core team member, captured the priority question in a remark The Register quoted about SQL Property Graph Queries (SQL/PGQ): "At this point I'd be willing to bet dinner that if we ship it in v19 there will be post-release bug discoveries that are unfixable until v20." Whether you can fix a defect after release is what decides its priority. 4. Split Must-Fix From Follow-Up My bug triage table sorts defect reports into five buckets: must-fix, fix if cheap, follow-up, design call and close. The Postgres 19 examples come from the PostgreSQL 19 Open Items wiki page and Tomas Vondra's analysis. The buckets are my own call, not the project's. Bucket What goes in it Postgres 19 example Decision before the release date Must-fix Wrong results, data loss, security, crashes, anything you can't fix after release "REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) loses missing values of columns added without a rewrite" Fix and add a test, or revert the feature Fix if cheap Real defect, small blast radius, small fix "COPY (query) TO ... (FORMAT json) uses the table's column names" Batch into the cluster's fix series Follow-up Real, contained, fixable in a minor release without a behavior change "psql backslash commands fail with translated messages and a non UTF-8 client encoding" File it, tag it, schedule it Design call The defect points at a design flaw UPDATE/DELETE FOR PORTION OF, where Tomas Vondra notes the concurrency issue was known and documented with a workaround Revert, or ship as experimental if your project allows it Close Duplicate, intended behavior, can't reproduce A report repeating an older finding Close with a one-line reason Design-call defects, the ones that point at a design flaw, are where Postgres 19 had no good option. Peter Eisentraut, a PostgreSQL core team member, wrote that the PostgreSQL community has discussed committing features with an "experimental" status, but hasn't "figured out a way to do this" yet. If your project has feature flags or preview labels, design-call defects are what they're for. The bug triage decision tree turns the five buckets into four questions in order: can it corrupt or leak data, can we fix it after release, is the fix small, and does it point at the design? The "long tail of relatively harmless issues" Peter Eisentraut described would mostly exit at the third question. 5. Do the Hours Math Before Anyone Starts Fixing Once every cluster of defect reports has a bucket, I'd do the hours math out loud in the triage meeting. My rough numbers per report: The fix: about 20 minutes for a three-line change. The overhead: about two more hours to reproduce it, write a test, get review and commit. The total: at about two hours and 20 minutes per report, 40 defect reports cost about 90 hours. If two people have three weeks of part-time attention, 90 hours is tight but doable for must-fix and fix-if-cheap. If the must-fix list includes a design flaw, the math says revert. Better to say it in week one than in week three. 6. Move Review Earlier So the List Doesn't Land at the End The real fix for a late pile of defect reports is upstream. The revert chart from Tomas Vondra, a PostgreSQL major contributor, shows the Postgres 19 problem was timing: the review happened, it just happened late. One defect costs very different amounts at two points in the cycle: Found before commit: one person, a few minutes. Found in beta: a thread, a reviewer and a release slot. Catching defects before commit is the whole argument for shift-left code review : run review on the diff while the author still has context. Peter Eisentraut, a PostgreSQL core team member, reached a similar conclusion for Postgres, writing that LLM-assisted fuzzing "probably needs to be part of feature development in the future." Liz Fong-Jones, Technical Fellow at Honeycomb, described moving review earlier on The Agentic Review podcast in September. Her team is doing "peer reviews sooner, doing peer reviews more often at the design stage." People review the design. Machines catch the off-by-one. A Short Bug Triage Workflow for AI Review Findings Here's the seven-step bug triage workflow I'd pin in the team channel. It fits in one afternoon for 40 AI review defect reports. Collect. Put every finding in one tracker view with one label, for example ai-review . Cluster. Merge duplicates and group by feature and root cause. Score. Give each cluster a blast radius (Large, Medium, Small) and a yes or no for "fixable after release." Bucket. Sort clusters into must-fix, fix if cheap, follow-up, design call or close. Do the math. Hours needed for must-fix plus fix-if-cheap, against hours left. If it doesn't fit, cut or revert now. Assign. One owner per cluster, one fix series per cluster. Feed it back. For every must-fix, write down which earlier check would have caught it, and add that check before the next freeze. If your AI review findings live in GitHub issues, this GitHub CLI command pulls every open ai-review issue into a file you can sort: gh issue list --label "ai-review" --state open --limit 200 \ --json number,title,labels,createdAt > triage.json Step 7, feeding each must-fix back into an earlier check, is the one teams skip. It's also the only step that makes next release's list of defect reports shorter. Our code review best practices guide has more on picking where review depth goes. The loop diagram shows the seven bug triage steps as a cycle, not a line. The arrow from "feed it back" returns to the start of the next release, which is how the list of defect reports shrinks over time. Where Qodo Fits in Bug Triage for AI Review Findings With AI code review, catching bugs isn't the hard part anymore. Postgres 19 had plenty of real findings. The hard part was ranking them by impact and deciding what ships, with the same few senior people doing all of it. Ranking review findings by impact is the problem we build for at Qodo . Qodo PR Triage ranks open pull requests with priority rules that combine high-severity review findings with blast radius: Medium blast radius means a change reaches another repository rated Critical or High. Large blast radius means a change reaches several repositories or blocks other PRs. Qodo's Software Map shows downstream dependents and tracks each finding as fixed before merge, dismissed or shipped unfixed, which matches the must-fix versus follow-up split in my bug triage table. Itamar Friedman, co-founder and CEO of Qodo, called out blast radius estimation on the September episode of The Agentic Review with Liz Fong-Jones: "maybe estimate what is the blast radius of a change, like, try to estimate a severity. I almost feel like it's an underrated killer feature of AI." Conclusion: Bug Triage Is the Bottleneck Now Postgres 19 is a good release story to learn from because the defects were real and the people were excellent. AI-assisted review raised the bar on code that was written before the bar moved, and review that ran late left little time to clear the list. When you get your own 40 reports, cluster them, rank by blast radius, split severity from priority and do the hours math early. Then move review to where the author still has context, so the next list is shorter. How does your team triage a pile of AI review findings before a release? I'd love to hear in the comments. FAQ About Bug Triage and AI Code Review What is bug triage? Bug triage is the process of deciding what happens to each defect report: fix now, fix later, redesign or close. You check that the report is real, group duplicates, rate severity and priority, and assign an owner. Qodo adds blast radius and review findings to each pull request, so triage starts from impact. Why was Postgres 19 delayed? Postgres 19 was delayed after 8 to 10 significant features were reverted late in beta, and on October 10th the release team moved GA to November 19 to include more back-branch fixes. Peter Eisentraut, a PostgreSQL core team member, points partly to LLM-assisted review finding a long tail of edge-case defects. Tomas Vondra, a PostgreSQL major contributor, found that most reverts came from human review, much of it late. Could AI code review findings create another triage bottleneck? AI code review findings can create a triage bottleneck when they arrive in bulk near a deadline, because each report has fixed processing overhead. Clustering by root cause and ranking by blast radius keeps the overhead under control. Qodo PR Triage combines high-severity findings with blast radius and SLA (service level agreement) rules, so reviewers see the risky changes first. How do we manage human review capacity when code output grows? Manage human review capacity by spending people on design and high blast radius changes, and letting automated review handle routine defects. Liz Fong-Jones, Technical Fellow at Honeycomb, said on The Agentic Review that treating everything as important means "nothing is important." Qodo runs review on every pull request and ranks the queue, so human attention goes where impact is highest. What is the difference between severity vs priority in bug triage? Severity vs priority in bug triage comes down to impact versus timing. Severity measures how bad a defect is, while priority measures how soon you'll fix it. A deadline can lower the priority of a severe bug in a feature you plan to revert. Qodo's blast radius labels give you a consistent severity signal across pull requests. What else should we test after a change that AI review flags? After AI review flags a change, test the downstream code that depends on it, beyond the changed component. List the services, schemas and contracts the change touches, then pick tests for each. Qodo's Software Map shows downstream dependents and service contracts across repositories, so you can scope those tests.

title: Hivemind: shared memory for coding agents, built on FalkorDB
author: Jaskaran
summary: On many teams, each developer now works with their own coding agent: Claude Code, Kiro, Codex or something else. These agents don't share anything with each other. One agent doesn't know what another is changing, and each session starts without any memory of earlier ones. If one agent found yesterday that an approach breaks the tests, another agent may try the same approach today. For Graph Hacks (WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB) I built Hivemind , a shared memory that all of these agents read from and write to. It is stored as a graph in FalkorDB. This post explains the problem, how the system works, the main Cypher queries, and what I learned while building it. There is a live demo that runs in the browser without sign-up. I refer to specific steps of it below: hivemind-live-demo.vercel.app Quantapixel / hivemind Hivemind: a shared graph brain for every coding agent on a team (Claude Code, Kiro, Codex). Built on FalkorDB for Graph Hacks. ⬡ Hivemind A shared graph brain for every coding agent on a team. Built on FalkorDB for Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents (WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB, Oct 15–18 2026). ▶ Live demo hivemind-live-demo.vercel.app : press Play, no sign-up Demo videos Hivemind demo (3:14) · Walkthrough of the live demo (2:49) Track Agent Memory and Coordination (Track 02) Built with FalkorDB Cloud · Python · MCP · Claude Code, Kiro and Codex hooks · Vercel Five developers each run their own Claude Code, Codex or Kiro agent on the same repo. None of those agents knows what the others are doing. Agent A rewrites validate_token() while Agent B builds on its old behaviour. Agent C retries a fix that Agent D found breaks production yesterday. Every session starts from zero. Hivemind puts every agent on one graph. It holds the code's call graph, who is changing what, what has been tried… View on GitHub The problem The demo uses a fictional team of five working on a small shop backend: Priya (tech lead, Claude Code), Marco (Kiro), Aisha (Codex), Ken (Claude Code) and Lena (Kiro). Marco asks Kiro to add JWT support, and Kiro starts changing validate_token() in shop/tokens.py . Shortly after, Aisha asks Codex to add rate limiting to checkout() in shop/orders.py . These are different files, but checkout() calls current_user() , which calls validate_token() . Aisha's change depends on code that Marco is changing at the same time. Which of these would Git catch? None of them. Marco and Aisha edit different files, so there is no merge conflict. Marco's failed attempt is never committed. Priya's earlier decision that tokens must stay HMAC-signed until the mobile v3 app ships isn't in Git either. Git tracks changes to text, and these problems are about how the code is connected and what the team already knows. Later, Marco's first approach (replacing the HMAC check with a PyJWT decode) fails test_refresh_session , because users with old tokens get logged out. A second try fails the same way. He stops for the day, and the next morning Lena continues the task with an agent that has none of this information. Existing approaches cover parts of this. Git and code review find problems after the work is done. CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files are written by hand and don't reflect work in progress. Each agent's own memory stays on one machine and inside one tool. Asking teammates in chat depends on people remembering to ask. Approach: attach memory to the code Most of the information worth sharing is about a specific function: who is changing validate_token , what was tried on it, and which decisions apply to it. So Hivemind attaches each piece of memory to the functions it is about. Functions are connected by calls. That means the question "what should my agent know before editing checkout ?" becomes "what is connected to checkout ?", which is a graph traversal. The other questions an agent needs answered have the same form: Is anyone changing code that mine calls? Follow CALLS edges until reaching a teammate's claim. What has been tried near this function? Look one hop out for attempts. What could break if I change it? Follow callers backwards. In SQL these would be recursive joins on every agent step. In Cypher each one is a short query, and FalkorDB returns them quickly enough to run before every edit. Some other FalkorDB features were useful: Multi-graph support. Each team gets its own graph ( hivemind_shop , hivemind_payments ) in one database. Built-in algorithms. algo.pageRank , algo.betweenness and shortestPath power the dashboard. Redis protocol and a free cloud tier. Every agent connects to the database directly, so there is no separate Hivemind server. The data model The graph has two layers. The code layer is parsed from the repository. The team memory layer records what people and agents did, linked to the relevant functions. In the example: Marco ran a Kiro session that works on the task "Add JWT support". The task claims validate_token , which records who is currently changing it. The session made an attempt that failed twice and touched validate_token . Later, Lena's passing attempt resolves that failure, and her decision supersedes Priya's earlier one. The code layer is built with Python's ast module. It records every function, the functions it calls, and each file's imports, and writes them in batches using UNWIND and MERGE . Each function also stores a hash of its syntax tree, without line numbers. When an agent edits a file, Hivemind re-indexes only that file and compares the hashes, which shows exactly which functions changed. Formatting changes and comment edits don't change the hash. Logic changes do. How function calls are resolved When a function calls validate_token , the indexer needs to decide which validate_token is meant. It prefers one defined in the same file, and otherwise uses any function with that name: MATCH ( a: Function { file: $file }) UNWIND a.calls AS name MATCH ( b: Function { name: name }) WHERE b <> a WITH a , collect ( b ) AS targets , [ t IN collect ( b ) WHERE t.file = a.file ] AS local UNWIND CASE WHEN size ( local ) > 0 THEN local ELSE targets END AS t MERGE ( a ) - [ :CALLS ] -> ( t ) This is not a type checker, and dynamic dispatch can mislead it. For typical application code it is accurate enough, and it is cheap to rerun after each edit. Detecting conflicts before an edit Before an agent edits a file, a hook checks whether any of the functions being changed are within three calls of a function that a teammate has claimed: MATCH ( t: Function ) WHERE t.qname IN $mine MATCH p = ( t ) - [ :CALLS * 1 .. 3 ] -> ( o: Function ) <- [ :CLAIMS ] - ( i: Intent { status: 'active' }) WHERE i.dev <> $me RETURN t.qname , o.qname , i.dev , i.description , [ n IN nodes ( p ) | n.qname ] AS path [:CALLS*1..3] matches paths of one to three call edges. nodes(p) returns the path itself, so the agent can show the developer how the two pieces of code are connected. The full check runs three variants: The same function Code that my code calls Code that calls my code For each pair it keeps the shortest path, which is the easiest to read. If a conflict is found, the hook pauses the edit once and returns the explanation to the agent, which passes it on to the developer. If the developer continues, the next attempt goes through. The acknowledgement is stored as a node so the same warning isn't shown again. I chose a one-time warning over a hard block, because a hard block would get in the way of normal work. In the demo: press Next step until step 4 ("Aisha starts rate limiting in Codex"). A red path appears between checkout and validate_token . Recording memory automatically The first version gave agents MCP tools such as record_attempt and relied on them to call these tools. In practice they rarely did, because they focus on the task they were given. The memory stayed mostly empty. I moved recording into hooks, which Claude Code, Kiro and Codex all support. The hooks run at fixed points: When the agent receives a prompt, it becomes the session's task. Before an edit, the functions being edited are claimed and checked for conflicts. After an edit, the file is re-indexed and the changed functions are recorded. When tests run after code changes, the result is recorded as an attempt on those functions. When the agent stops, its summary is saved as the task's progress note. For example, Marco's failure is recorded like this: The prompt "Add JWT support to auth tokens" becomes a task. Kiro edits tokens.py . Re-indexing shows that the hash of validate_token changed. Kiro runs pytest . The exit code is 1, and test_refresh_session is read from the output. The changed function and the failing test become an Attempt linked to validate_token . If Kiro then describes the failure in its own words, that description is added to the same attempt instead of creating a second one. Handling three different hook formats Claude Code sends PascalCase events ( PreToolUse , PostToolUseFailure ), and its tools are called Edit , Write and Bash . Kiro sends camelCase events ( preToolUse , agentSpawn ). Its tools are called fs_write and execute_bash , and it puts the exit status in tool_response.result[0] . Codex uses Claude-style event names, but its tool names differ between versions ( shell , exec_command , apply_patch ). So edits and commands are identified by their inputs instead of by tool name. A small normalisation layer converts all of these into one event format. I based it on payloads captured from real sessions, which are now used as test fixtures, because the documentation didn't cover every case. Test runs are detected by matching the command ( pytest , unittest , jest , go test , cargo test and others) and checking the exit code. The name of the failing test is then parsed from the output. Before an agent edits a function, it receives everything that was tried on that function or its direct neighbours: MATCH ( t: Function ) WHERE t.qname IN $q MATCH ( t ) - [ :CALLS * 0 .. 1 ] - ( fn: Function ) <- [ :TOUCHED ] - ( a: Attempt ) RETURN a.summary , a.outcome , a.reason , a.count , a.devs , a.resolved When Lena's agent opens validate_token , its context includes the fact that the PyJWT decode failed twice, and why. Consolidating memory If every event became a new node, the memory would fill up with near-duplicates. Hivemind merges related entries when it writes them. Repeated failures merge. If a new attempt has the same outcome on the same code, with the same failing tests or very similar wording, the existing attempt's count is increased instead of adding a node. Fixes resolve failures. When tests pass on code with open failures, those failures are marked as fixed and linked to the fix with a RESOLVES edge. They stay in the graph as history. Decisions supersede decisions. A new decision on the same code SUPERSEDES the old one. Agents see only the current decision, while why() can still show the earlier ones. Query: a passing attempt resolves earlier failures MATCH ( f: Attempt { outcome: 'failed' }) - [ :TOUCHED ] -> ( fn: Function ) WHERE fn.qname IN $q AND coalesce ( f.resolved , false ) = false WITH DISTINCT f MATCH ( a: Attempt { id: $fix }) CREATE ( a ) - [ :RESOLVES ] -> ( f ) SET f.resolved = true , f.resolved_dev = $dev DISTINCT is needed because one failure can touch several of the functions in $q . Without it, duplicate RESOLVES edges would be created. In the demo: step 7 ("Marco tries again, same failure") shows the merged failure with a ×2 badge. Step 10 ("Lena ships the fix") shows it marked as fixed by Lena. Handoffs When Marco stops, his agent hands the task off with a note. When Lena resumes it, one query moves the OWNS edge to her and links her session to the task. Everything else stays connected to the task: the claims, Marco's sessions, both failed attempts, his note and Priya's decision. Lena's agent receives the full history in one call. The resume query MATCH ( i: Intent { id: $task }) OPTIONAL MATCH ( :Developer ) - [ o: OWNS ] -> ( i ) DELETE o WITH DISTINCT i MATCH ( d: Developer { name: $me }), ( s: Session { id: $session }) CREATE ( d ) - [ :OWNS ] -> ( i ) CREATE ( s ) - [ :WORKS_ON ] -> ( i ) SET i.status = 'active' Querying the memory Agents also get an MCP server with 14 tools, for things the hooks can't infer: starting and handing off tasks, recording decisions and conventions, and answering questions about the code. Three of these tools explain the code, and each is a single traversal: blast_radius follows callers backwards: MATCH p = ( caller: Function ) - [ :CALLS * 1 .. 3 ] -> ( t: Function { qname: $q }) RETURN caller.qname , min ( length ( p )) AS distance who_knows ranks developers by their claims, attempts and decisions on a function and its neighbours. why returns the current decision, the decision it replaced, all attempts, and the people involved. At the end of the demo, why("validate_token") returns the full history of the JWT change. In the demo: at step 12, click validate_token on the map. The panel on the right shows the same information as why . The dashboard The dashboard shows the codebase as a map: Functions are grouped by file. Each developer's work is outlined in their colour. Conflict paths are drawn in red. Memory is shown as badges on functions. It uses FalkorDB's algorithms in a few places: algo.pageRank ranks functions that much of the code depends on. algo.betweenness finds functions that many call paths pass through, which is where conflicts are more likely. The path finder uses shortestPath . When two functions aren't directly connected, it shows their closest shared caller instead. People can also add decisions and conventions from the dashboard. Architecture and setup Each agent connects to FalkorDB Cloud directly over Cypher, through both the hooks and the MCP server. The dashboard is hosted on Vercel, reads the same graph, and is protected by an access code. Timestamps come from the database server's clock, since laptop clocks can differ. To join a team, you install Hivemind with uv tool install git+https://github.com/Quantapixel/hivemind and run hivemind join <dashboard-url> inside the project. The command: Asks for the team's access code Detects which agents are installed Configures each agent in its own format Indexes the code hivemind doctor checks the setup and reports what to fix. Source code is not uploaded. The graph stores function names, how functions call each other, and what people did to them. Testing with real agents I tested Hivemind with three separate clones of a project, acting as three machines that shared one cloud graph. First, Kira (using Kiro) was asked to add token revocation. The prompt didn't mention Hivemind. The hooks recorded the task, revoke_token as added, validate_token as changed, the passing test run, and Kiro's summary. Next, Carl (using Claude Code) was asked to add token scopes in the same area. During the task, his agent noted: "The revocation check from kira's recent change is untouched." It had picked up Kira's change from the shared memory without being asked to check. Finally, Cody (using Codex) read the shared task board through MCP and saw both of their tasks. What I learned Agents don't reliably record things themselves. Relying on agents to call a recording tool left the memory mostly empty. Recording through hooks, outside the agent's decisions, worked much better. The first conflict query was too broad. It followed CALLS edges in both directions in one pattern, so two functions were flagged as conflicting just because a third function called both. Splitting it into "code I call" and "code that calls me" removed these false positives and made the explanations clearer. Re-indexing could delete memory. Developers' working copies differ, so a function missing from one copy may still exist on another branch. Early on, re-indexing one copy could delete that function and the memory attached to it. Now a function is only removed if no memory is attached to it. Documentation didn't cover all hook payloads. The first real Kiro and Claude Code sessions each found cases my hand-written test fixtures had missed. The hook tests now use payloads captured from real sessions, and all tests run against a real FalkorDB instance. Region placement matters. The dashboard was first deployed in a region far from the database, which made every request slow. Deploying it in the same region as the database fixed this. Overall, the graph model kept the code small. Conflict detection, context, consolidation, handoffs, blast radius, who_knows and why are each one or two Cypher queries. Next steps Support for TypeScript, Go and Rust using Tree-sitter (only Python is indexed now) Merging similar failures by meaning using FalkorDB's vector index (currently it uses word overlap) Linking decisions to pull requests automatically Suggesting reviewers using community detection on the call graph Expiring old attempts and stale claims Try it The live demo plays through the full scenario step by step. There is also a 3-minute video using real agents. To run it locally without any accounts: git clone https://github.com/Quantapixel/hivemind && cd hivemind && uv sync docker compose up -d # local FalkorDB uv run hivemind ui & # http://127.0.0.1:8765 uv run hivemind demo --step # press Enter to advance If your team uses several agents on one codebase, I'd be interested to hear how you coordinate them. Built for Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents (WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB, October 2026), Track 02: Agent Memory and Coordination. I built it with Claude Code as my coding assistant: the idea and product direction are mine, and much of the code was written by the assistant under that direction and reviewed by me. All example data is synthetic.

title: Perplexity, Burstiness, and AI Text Detection: An NLP Glossary
author: Wajahat Ali Shahani
summary: What do "perplexity," "burstiness," and "watermarking" actually mean when people throw them around in AI-detection debates? We wrote a plain-English glossary of the core NLP vocabulary, grounded in the primary papers. Here is the short version of the terms that matter most, with why each one is in the conversation. Perplexity Perplexity measures how "surprised" a language model is by a text: the average probability it assigns to each next token, inverted. Low perplexity means the text reads as highly predictable to a model. Because model-generated text tends to be fluent and statistically bland, detectors and researchers often treat very low perplexity as a machine-likeness signal. The Google ML Glossary defines it as "a measurement of how well a probability model predicts a sample." Caveat: careful, edited human prose - legal writing, textbook prose, some Wikipedia intros - also scores low on perplexity. Low perplexity is a register signal, not proof of authorship. (We saw exactly this failure mode in our 8-text detector test : a human Wikipedia paragraph scored 99% AI.) Burstiness Burstiness describes variation in sentence length and structure across a text - the rhythm of a human draft: some terse sentences, some long winding ones. Classical work by Benedetto, Caglioti, and Loreto (Physical Review Letters, 2002) showed that compressed-length features of human language vary in characteristic ways that simple generated text does not. Modern detectors use stylistic features in this family; when people say detectors look for "human rhythm," burstiness is usually what they mean. Tokenization Models do not read words; they read subword units produced by tokenizers (BPE, WordPiece). Detectors that operate on token probabilities inherit everything about how the tokenizer splits text - which is partly why detector behavior shifts across languages and domains. Watermarking Green et al. (2023) proposed embedding statistical "green lists" of plausible next tokens during generation, so watermarked text carries a detectable signature. Kirchenbauer et al. (arXiv:2301.10226, ICML 2023) extended this to bit-encoded payloads. Watermarking is a provenance technique, not a detector of human text - and its signals can be attacked: Sadasivan et al. showed paraphrasing (including recursive paraphrasing) can substantially reduce watermark detectability (arXiv:2303.11156, TMLR). Membership inference & zero-shot detection Zero-shot detectors (Liang et al., arXiv:2304.02819, Patterns) estimate the likelihood a token sequence came from a model, without detector-specific training. The same paper found widely used detectors disproportionately mis-flagged non-native English writers - constrained prose reads as machine prose. GLTR & the original detector toolkit GLTR (Gehrmann, Strobelt, Rush; ACL 2019 demo, arXiv:1906.04043) visualizes token-rank distributions to help humans spot machine text. It is a teaching tool as much as a detector, and its paper is a clean entry point into the whole feature family. The honest takeaway Every term above describes a statistical property of text , and every detector is a model built on such properties. Confidence percentages describe the model, not the writer's laptop. The practical workflow is review, not screening. title: A crypto checkout with no backend: verifying a USDT payment from the browser
author: rene
summary: A crypto checkout with no backend: verifying a USDT payment from the browser Most e-commerce checkouts require a heavy stack: a database to store orders, a server to handle logic, and a way to listen to blockchain events. But what if you could build a fully functional service store using only a static site? In this article, I’ll walk through how the crypto-store handles payments. We aren't using a traditional backend to watch for transaction events. Instead, we use a "balance-delta" method—verifying a USDT (BEP-20) payment directly from the visitor's browser using a public RPC. The Architecture: No Backend, No Problem When a user visits the store to order a service (like an AI code review or a landing page), the site needs to know if they actually sent the money. Usually, this requires a backend to index blockchain events. Instead, we use a Client-Side Balance Check . Here is the logic: The Baseline: When the user initiates an order, the app performs an eth_call to get the current USDT balance of the store's wallet. The Watchdog (Polling): Once the baseline is set, the browser doesn't just sit idle. It initiates a polling loop. Every 20 seconds, the app sends a new eth_call using the balanceOf selector ( 0x70a08231 ) to check the current USDT balance of the store's wallet. The Verification: The app calculates the difference between the new balance and the baseline. If that difference is greater than or equal to the quoted amount—with a 0.1% tolerance to account for any minor rounding or precision issues—the payment is flagged as "Paid" in the browser. The TTL (Time-to-Live): To prevent the app from waiting indefinitely, the check expires after 60 minutes. If the payment isn't detected within this window, the session expires. The "Honesty" Disclaimer: Why this isn't a perfect automated system While this method is incredibly efficient for a static site, it isn't without its quirks. Because we are using a "balance-delta" check (looking at how much the total wallet balance increased) rather than looking for a specific transaction hash, there are two things you should know: The Concurrent Buyer Risk: If two people pay at the exact same moment, the app might see a single large jump in the wallet balance and attribute it incorrectly. This is a known technical limitation of using a single wallet for multiple simultaneous orders. The Human-in-the-Loop: Because of the reason above, the "Paid" status in your browser is a convenience , not a final legal contract. To ensure 100% accuracy, the owner manually verifies every transaction on BscScan before beginning any work. Delivery & Refunds Because this is a service-based store (offering things like AI code reviews and landing page builds), the process isn't instant: Delivery: Once your payment is confirmed, your service will be delivered via email or Telegram within 24-48 hours . Refunds: All sales are final. There are no refunds, so please ensure you are sending USDT on the BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20) . Sending USDT on any other network (like Ethereum or Polygon) will result in lost funds.
